# Gram-positive cocci

> *Staphylococci and streptococci cause a bewildering range of illness, from a boil to food
> poisoning to heart disease weeks after a sore throat. This chapter shows that a handful of traits,
> and three ways of causing harm, explain almost all of it.*

## One bacterium, three illnesses {#sec-gpc-hook}

Consider three people:

- A teenager scratches a mosquito bite. Two days later there is a hot, swollen, pus-filled lump.
- Forty wedding guests start vomiting two to three hours after lunch. Most are well by the next day.
- A young woman suddenly develops a high fever, a rash and dangerously low blood pressure.

The same organism, *Staphylococcus aureus*, can cause all three. That sounds like three facts to
memorise. It is really one organism using three different mechanisms, and by the end of this
chapter you should be able to explain each from how the bacterium works.

## The group in one sentence {#sec-gpc-sentence}

**Gram-positive cocci are thick-walled spheres that live on our skin and mucous membranes, and cause
harm mainly when they get past a barrier.** Here are the book's six questions, answered for the whole
group. The rest of the chapter is about how its members give different answers to the fifth.

| Question | Answer for the Gram-positive cocci |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | Thick peptidoglycan wall, no outer membrane (so no LPS); many have a capsule or surface proteins that resist phagocytes |
| How does it get energy? | Staphylococci respire or ferment; streptococci and enterococci only ferment, but tolerate oxygen |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; swaps genes readily, which is how toxin genes and resistance spread |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Skin, nose, throat, mouth and gut of healthy people; spread by hands, droplets and contact |
| How does damage happen? | Three patterns: invasion with pus, toxins, and immune-mediated damage (see below) |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall, and the proteins that build it |

## Sorting the group {#sec-gpc-key}

A few traits separate every member of the group. The key below is how a laboratory sorts them, but
read each branch for what the trait *means* about the organism.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-key.yml"></div>

The key's three main organisms each get a profile card below. The others are supporting organisms,
covered in one table at the end.

## *Staphylococcus aureus*: three patterns of harm {#sec-gpc-aureus}

*S. aureus* lives in the nose of about one in three healthy people at any one time
[@kluytmans1997carriage]. It carries an unusually large toolkit: coagulase, enzymes that damage
tissue, and many toxins. Different tools produce different illnesses.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Invasion with pus | Enters through a break in skin; coagulase walls it in fibrin; neutrophils pour in | An abscess or boil |
| Toxin without invasion | Grows in food left warm and releases a **heat-stable** toxin; the toxin, not the bacteria, makes people ill | Vomiting within hours of a meal [@argudin2010enterotoxins] |
| Toxin acting on the whole body | A **superantigen** switches on a huge fraction of the body's T cells at once | Toxic shock: fever, rash and collapsing blood pressure [@llewelyn2002superantigens] |

These are the three people in the opening. The first is an infection. The second is not an infection
at all: the guests swallowed toxin that was already in the food. In the third, the host's own immune
response does most of the damage.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

Its quieter relative lives on everyone's skin and causes trouble in a completely different way.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-saureus-sepidermidis.yml"></div>

## *Streptococcus pyogenes*: weapons and a delayed attack {#sec-gpc-pyogenes}

*S. pyogenes*, or group A streptococcus, lives on the throat and skin. Where *S. aureus* walls itself
in, *S. pyogenes* breaks barriers down, and some of its worst effects come after the infection has gone.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Spread through tissue | Enzymes dissolve clots, DNA and the gel between cells | Spreading infection of skin |
| Toxins | Streptolysins burst cells; superantigens like those of *S. aureus* | Scarlet fever; streptococcal toxic shock |
| Immune-mediated damage, weeks later | Antibodies against the bacterium cross-react with the host's own tissues (molecular mimicry) | Rheumatic fever, which can scar heart valves [@carapetis2016rheumatic] |

The third pattern is the clearest example in this book of the damage-response idea from general
pathology: the bacteria are long gone, and the host's immune system causes the damage.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pyogenes.yml"></div>

## *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: armour {#sec-gpc-pneumoniae}

*S. pneumoniae* has fewer weapons. Its strength is its **capsule**, a slippery polysaccharide coat that
stops phagocytes engulfing it. Many healthy young children carry it in the nose and throat
[@weiser2018pneumococcus]. Disease starts when it reaches a space next door, or the blood, and multiplies
there.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Multiplying where it does not belong | The capsule resists phagocytes; the host's inflammation fills the space | Infection of the middle ear, sinuses or lung |
| Invasion of blood and meninges | Capsule protection in the bloodstream, worst when host defences are weak | Bloodstream infection, meningitis |

The capsule also explains protection. Antibodies that coat the capsule let phagocytes engulf the
bacteria, so pneumococcal vaccines are built from capsule material. Because the capsule comes in about
100 types, vaccines include the commonest ones.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

The two streptococci make a useful pair, because they show two broad ways any pathogen can cause harm.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-pyogenes-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

## Supporting organisms {#sec-gpc-supporting}

These organisms matter, but each can be understood as a variation on the main three. Learn the
separating trait and the reason it matters; the organ-system blocks will add the rest.

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Staphylococcus epidermidis* and other coagulase-negative staphylococci | Everyone's skin | No coagulase; few toxins; forms biofilm on plastic and metal | Infects devices such as catheters and artificial joints; contaminates blood samples [@otto2009epidermidis] |
| *Streptococcus agalactiae* (group B) | Gut and vagina of about one in five pregnant women [@russell2017gbs] | Beta-haemolytic, Lancefield group B | Harmless to most adults; dangerous to newborns, who meet it at birth with immature defences |
| Viridans streptococci | Mouth | Alpha-haemolytic, no large capsule | Some ferment sugar to acid that dissolves tooth enamel; in the blood, they can stick to damaged heart valves |
| *Enterococcus* | Gut | Tolerates bile and salt; naturally resistant to several drugs | Persists in hospitals; strains with acquired resistance are hard to treat |

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "*S. aureus* is a hospital superbug"
Most *S. aureus* is not a superbug, and most of it is not in hospitals: it lives harmlessly in the noses
of about one in three people. **MRSA** is *S. aureus* that has **acquired a gene** for an altered version
of the protein that a whole family of drugs targets, so the drugs bind it poorly
[@lakhundi2018mrsa]. Resistance is a trait some strains carry, not a property of the species, and it
spread because drug use selected for the bacteria that already had it. The genetics chapter explains how.
:::

## Later in the course {#sec-gpc-later}

You will meet these organisms again. When you do, place each new fact on the profile cards above.

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *S. aureus* | Skin and soft tissue, bone and joint, and heart valve infections; food safety; MRSA in pharmacology |
| *S. epidermidis* | Infections of devices and implants |
| *S. pyogenes* | Throat and skin infections; rheumatic heart disease in the cardiovascular block |
| *S. pneumoniae* | Ear, sinus, lung and meningeal infections; vaccines in immunology |
| *S. agalactiae* | Infections of newborns; screening in pregnancy |
| Viridans streptococci | Dental decay; heart valve infection |
| *Enterococcus* | Urinary and hospital-acquired infections; resistance in pharmacology |
